label: Lie Groups and Algebras
notes: Welcome to Appendix 12. We are assembling the language that lets symmetry and dynamics meet: a Lie group is simultaneously a smooth manifold and a group. By the end you should see why the rigid body and the perfect fluid live naturally on coadjoint orbits, and why the exponential map is the bridge from the algebra back to the group.

label: What is a Lie Group
notes: Stress the double structure here. Multiplication and inversion are not just abstractly defined; they are smooth maps of manifolds. That smoothness is what allows us to differentiate the group operations and extract an algebra. Point out that the dimension of the manifold equals the number of continuous parameters describing a group element.

label: Examples of Lie Groups
notes: Walk through each example as a manifold and a group at once. SO(3) is the configuration space of a rotating rigid body; SU(2) double covers it and runs the spin story; SE(3) handles full rigid motion in space; GL(n) is the open ambient group inside which the others sit. Emphasize their dimensions out loud.

label: The Lie Algebra
notes: The key move: differentiate the manifold at the identity. The tangent space there is a vector space of the right dimension, and we call it the Lie algebra. Make clear that the identity is special because translation by any group element carries it everywhere, so the whole group looks locally like this one tangent space.

label: Left-Invariant Vector Fields
notes: Explain why a single tangent vector at the identity spreads to an entire vector field. Left translation is a diffeomorphism, so pushing the vector forward gives a left-invariant field that is determined everywhere by its value at e. This identification is what turns the tangent space into something with extra algebraic structure.

label: The Lie Bracket
notes: Introduce the commutator as the operation that makes the tangent space an algebra rather than just a vector space. Antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity are the two axioms to remember. For matrix groups the bracket is literally XY minus YX, which students can compute by hand, anchoring the abstraction in arithmetic.

label: One-Parameter Subgroups
notes: A one-parameter subgroup is a smooth homomorphism from the real line into the group. Each element X of the algebra generates exactly one such curve, the integral curve of its left-invariant field through the identity. Emphasize the homomorphism property: the curve at time s plus t equals the product of its values at s and t.

label: The Exponential Map
notes: This is the central picture. The exponential map sends a straight line through the origin of the algebra to a one-parameter subgroup threading the identity of the group. For matrices it is the familiar power series. Near the identity it is a local diffeomorphism, giving canonical coordinates of the first kind.

label: The Bracket as Non-Commutativity
notes: Make the parallelogram concrete. Flow along X, then Y, then back along X, then back along Y; in a non-abelian group you do not return to the start. The leading discrepancy is exactly the bracket of X and Y, scaled by the time squared. The bracket measures the failure of the flows to commute.

label: Adjoint Representation
notes: Conjugation by a group element acts on the algebra; its derivative at the identity is the adjoint representation Ad. Differentiating Ad in the group variable produces the lowercase ad, and ad of X is just bracket with X. Tie this chain together slowly: it links group conjugation, algebra automorphisms, and the bracket into one structure.

label: Coadjoint Orbits and Mechanics
notes: Close on the payoff for mechanics. The coadjoint action lives on the dual of the algebra, and its orbits carry a natural symplectic structure, the Kirillov form. The rigid body's angular momentum sphere and the Euler equations of fluids are coadjoint orbits. This is where symmetry becomes Hamiltonian dynamics.
